Runs as is. Output:

pad all to 4096: waste 59.6%
pad per micro-batch of 2: waste 35.7%
packed rows: [[4000], [3100, 700], [2200, 1500, 300], [1000, 450]]
naive tokens per rank: 8900 4350
balanced tokens per rank: [6650, 6600]

blocks.md: Packing within a GPU is half the job. Data-parallel ranks meet at the gradient all-reduce, so every step waits for the rank with the most work. Split the 8 sequences by arrival order, 4 per rank, and rank 0 gets 8,900 tokens while rank 1 gets 4,350 and idles about half the time. Assigning longest first to the lighter rank gives 6,650 and 6,600. verl's trainer balances by default (`balance_batch`) with the Karmarkar-Karp partitioning method, and its balancing code estimates the workload of a sequence as $24576\,s + s^2$ for length $s$, because attention cost grows with the square of length; NeMo RL's dynamic batching strides length-sorted sequences across ranks. DeepSeek-R1's trainer does all three steps: sort the global batch by length and deal it across DP ranks, Best-Fit pack within each rank, then equalize the number of packed chunks per rank.

blocks.title: Tokens per data-parallel rank

scenes.caption: Arrival order: rank 0 holds A, B, C, D (8,900 tokens), rank 1 holds E to H (4,350). Rank 1 finishes early and waits at the all-reduce.
Balanced: rank 0 gets D, C, G, E and rank 1 gets A, F, H, B. Each then packs its own 4 sequences into 2 rows.

blocks.md: Packing has one trap. The token-mean loss is a sum over every loss token in the **global** batch divided by their count $N$. If each micro-batch instead takes its own mean and the gradients are averaged, a token's weight depends on who shares its row. Rank 0's rows above are [4000] and [1500, 700, 450] = 2650 tokens. Run each row as its own micro-batch: averaging the two micro-batch means weights each token of the second row by $1/(2 \times 2650)$ and each token of the first by $1/(2 \times 4000)$, 1.51x apart. Switching packing on reshuffles rows, so the gradient changes. The fix is to sum within each micro-batch and divide by the global token count: verl's `agg_loss` divides by the global `batch_num_tokens` (and multiplies by the DP size, because DDP averages across ranks) so the loss is invariant to the parallelism. Hugging Face Transformers shipped the same bug in gradient accumulation until 2024, when Unsloth and Benjamin Marie reported it and the team [fixed it](https://huggingface.co/blog/gradient_accumulation).

blocks.tex: \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{m}\sum_{t \in m} \ell_t}_{\text{correct: global token mean}} \quad\ne\quad \underbrace{\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m}\frac{1}{N_m}\sum_{t\in m}\ell_t}_{\text{mean of micro-batch means}}
blocks.caption: N is the number of loss tokens in the whole batch, M the number of micro-batches and N_m the tokens in micro-batch m. The two agree only when every micro-batch holds the same number of tokens, which packing never guarantees.

blocks.md: Very long responses need one more tool. *Context parallelism* (CP, megatron-core lesson 5) splits one sequence's tokens across GPUs and balances causal attention by cutting the sequence into $2 \times$ CP chunks, rank $r$ taking chunks $r$ and $2\,\text{CP} - 1 - r$. Packing breaks that recipe if the packed row is split as if it were one sequence, because the row holds several causal triangles that restart at every boundary. So NeMo RL CP-shards every sequence individually, padded to a multiple of $2 \times \text{CP} \times \text{TP}$, and then packs each rank's pieces. The logprob passes reuse all of this with their own, usually larger, token budgets (NeMo RL's `logprob_mb_tokens`, verl's `log_prob_max_token_len_per_gpu`), since a forward-only pass keeps no activations for backward.

blocks.title: Packing meets CP = 2: shard each sequence, not the row

scenes.caption: Sequences A (8 tokens) and B (4) packed into one row. Attention restarts at B, so B's first token attends to 1 key, not 9: the row holds two causal triangles.
Split the row as if it were one sequence (4 chunks of 3, CP0 takes chunks 0 and 3): CP0 reads 1+2+3 + 2+3+4 = 15 keys, CP1 reads 31. The balanced split assumed one triangle.
Per sequence: A in 4 chunks of 2, B in 4 chunks of 1, each rank taking chunks r and 3 - r of every sequence. CP0 reads 18 + 5 = 23 keys and CP1 23. Each rank then packs its own pieces.

blocks.md: Variable lengths waste trainer compute three ways: padding inside a row, empty rows, and idle ranks. Pack rows (with `cu_seqlens`), balance tokens across ranks, and normalize the loss by the global token count so none of this changes the gradient.

blocks.question: A team turns on sequence packing. Throughput doubles, but the loss curve shifts and the reward curve no longer matches the unpacked baseline. Which bug best explains it?
options: Packing changes the model's weights
FFD drops the longest sequences
The tokens moved to different GPUs, and floating point is not associative
The loss averages per-micro-batch means, so a token's weight depends on how many tokens share its row
blocks.explain: With a mean of micro-batch means, each token is weighted by 1 over its micro-batch's token count, and packing changes those counts. Dividing the summed loss by the global token count makes the gradient independent of how sequences are packed or split across ranks. Reduction-order noise is real but far too small to shift the curves.

blocks.question: Someone packs F (2200), C (1500) and B (300) into one row but runs plain causal attention over the row without `cu_seqlens`. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; causal masking already stops tokens from seeing other sequences
B's tokens attend to all of F and C and its positions start at 3700, so its logprobs differ from those of B alone
The row exceeds 4096 tokens
Only the last sequence's loss is computed
blocks.explain: A causal mask only hides future tokens. Without boundaries, every token of C and B also sees the earlier sequences in the row, and their position ids continue from the previous sequence. The trainer would then compute logprobs for contexts the policy never saw.

lessons.title: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step

blocks.md: After each optimizer step, the rollout engine holds stale weights. Syncing them has two parts: **resharding** (the trainer and engine split the model differently) and **transport** (moving the bytes). The bytes are easy to estimate: in BF16 the full model is 2 bytes per parameter. Qwen2.5-32B's checkpoint index lists 65,527,752,704 bytes (32.76B parameters); HybridFlow cites 140 GB for a 70B actor.

blocks.caption: B_eff is the bandwidth the transfer actually achieves. The estimate ignores latency, gather time and loading into the engine, so treat it as a lower bound.

blocks.md:
Worked numbers for Qwen2.5-32B (65.5 GB), at line rate (the link's full rated speed, the best case):

- **Through shared storage** at 5 GB/s (an assumed figure): write 13.1 s, read 13.1 s, so 26.2 s per step.
- **NCCL broadcast from one trainer rank** over one 400 Gb/s NIC (network interface card), which carries 400 gigabits per second, or 50 GB/s at 8 bits per byte: 1.31 s. A pipelined broadcast costs about the same however many receivers there are: NCCL cuts the tensor into chunks and passes them along a chain of GPUs, each forwarding one chunk while receiving the next, so every extra receiver adds only a small delay.
- **All 8 NICs of a trainer node** sending disjoint shards in parallel (400 GB/s): 0.164 s.

AReaL's cluster of NVIDIA H800 GPUs reports 3.2 Tb/s of inter-node bandwidth, with RDMA running over Ethernet, the same as 8 x 400 Gb/s NICs per node.

blocks.title: Full-weight sync time vs model size (BF16, line rate)

scenes.caption: At line rate, a 32B model syncs in 1.31 s over one NIC and 0.164 s over eight. Against a step of minutes, the network is rarely the problem by itself.
At half of line rate, every curve doubles. Going through storage adds tens of seconds per step for a 32B model, which is why systems stream weights directly between GPUs.

blocks.md: Measured costs are larger than these line-rate estimates, because transport is only part of the job: NeMo-Aligner's in-place TensorRT-LLM refit took 3.1 s per step for Llama 3 70B (5.8% of the step); HybridFlow reports baselines whose train-to-generate transition for 70B models took tens of seconds, and cut it by up to 89.1% (78.2 s); Kimi k1.5 reports under a minute from training to inference. The hard part is resharding.

**Why reshard?** Training wants large model parallelism for memory; generation is memory-bandwidth bound and prefers smaller tensor parallelism with more data-parallel replicas. HybridFlow measured that on 16 GPUs with training groups 1-8-2 (pipeline-tensor-data), using generation TP 2 for a 7B model and TP 4 for 13B cut generation latency by 60.3% and 36.4% compared with keeping TP 8. So the weights must be regrouped between phases.

The naive way all-gathers the full model on every GPU and then keeps the slice it needs. HybridFlow's 3D-HybridEngine (3D for the three parallelism dimensions: pipeline, tensor and data) instead chooses the generation groups so that each GPU's training shard is *part of* its generation shard, then all-gathers only within small *micro data-parallel* groups: the few GPUs whose training shards together make up one generation shard.

blocks.title: Resharding 8 GPUs: training TP 4 to generation TP 2 (HybridFlow)

scenes.caption: Training uses TP 4: groups G1-G4 and G5-G8 each split the weights into quarters s1 to s4, and DP pairs (G1, G5) hold the same quarter. Generation needs halves: A = s1 + s2 and B = s3 + s4.

Vanilla grouping uses consecutive ranks for generation TP: [G1, G2] get A and B. G2 holds s2 but needs B; G3 holds s3 but needs A. Those GPUs must keep a separate copy of their training shard: redundant memory.
HybridFlow picks generation TP groups at a stride ([G1, G3], [G2, G4], ...) so G1 and G2 both get A, which contains s1 and s2. Every training shard is reused in place.
Each GPU completes its half with one all-gather inside its micro DP group of 2: G1 fetches s2 from G2, G3 fetches s4 from G4. The four gathers run concurrently.

blocks.md: HybridFlow's Table 2 gives per-GPU transition costs for a model of size $M$ (bytes of weights) trained with $p$-$t$-$d$ groups ($p$ pipeline stages, $t$ tensor shards, $d$ data-parallel copies) and generated with $p_g$-$t_g$ groups. With Qwen2.5-7B ($M$ = 15.23 GB), training 1-8-2 on 16 GPUs and generation TP $t_g = 2$ ($p_g = 1$), each GPU holds a training shard of $M/(tp) = M/8$ and needs a generation shard of $M/(t_g p_g) = M/2$. HybridFlow fetches only the difference, $M/2 - M/8 = 3M/8 = 5.71$ GB; in general, the generation shard minus the training shard, $M/(t_g p_g) - M/(tp)$. The baselines rebuild the full model first, so they fetch everything except what they hold: DeepSpeed-Chat holds a 1/16 shard and fetches $15M/16 = 14.28$ GB; vanilla HybridFlow holds 1/8 and fetches $7M/8 = 13.33$ GB.

blocks.tex: V_{\text{DS-Chat}} = \tfrac{tpd-1}{tpd}M = 14.28\text{ GB},\quad V_{\text{HF-V}} = \tfrac{tp-1}{tp}M = 13.33\text{ GB},\quad V_{\text{HF}} = \tfrac{tp-t_g p_g}{t_g p_g\, tp}M = 5.71\text{ GB}
blocks.caption: Volume each GPU must gather. DeepSpeed-Chat all-gathers across all 16 GPUs; vanilla HybridFlow (HF-V) within training TP and PP groups; HybridFlow only within micro DP groups, the gap between its training and generation shards.

blocks.title: Per-GPU resharding cost, Qwen2.5-7B, 16 GPUs (Table 2 formulas)

scenes.caption: Communication volume per GPU: HybridFlow moves 5.71 GB, 2.5x less than DeepSpeed-Chat's full all-gather (14.28 GB).
Peak parameter memory per GPU during the transition: the baselines materialize the full model (15.23 GB); HybridFlow peaks at the generation shard, M / t_g = 7.62 GB.
Redundant memory (training weights that must be kept separately during generation): M/tpd = 0.95 GB, M/tp = 1.90 GB, and zero for HybridFlow.

blocks.md:
Transports in current frameworks (NeMo RL's refit guide lists them side by side):

- **Colocated**: CUDA IPC (inter-process communication) handles, which name a GPU buffer so another process on the same GPU can map it; the engine maps the trainer's GPU buffers without a network copy.
- **NCCL broadcast** of full tensors from trainer to every engine (NeMo RL's non-colocated default; SGLang's `init_weights_update_group` plus `update_weights_from_distributed`).
- **Shard-to-shard NCCL reshard**: each trainer rank sends only its shard and each engine rank receives only its own differently-parallelized shard. NeMo RL's profiling of large MoE models found the MoE FFN layers are 97% to 98% of the bytes.
- **Peer-to-peer RDMA**: Kimi k1.5 converts checkpoints to Hugging Face format (the standard checkpoint layout inference engines load) in shared memory and moves shards over RDMA with Mooncake (the transfer engine from Moonshot AI's serving platform).
- **Sparse deltas**: send only changed values, compressed, when the link is slow.

**A trillion-parameter case: Kimi K2's checkpoint engine.** K2 (1.04 trillion parameters, 32 billion active per token) trains colocated, and its report says a network file system is impractical at that scale. Instead, a *checkpoint engine* worker runs on every training node. To update, each one copies its node's local parameters from the training engine, then the **full** parameter set is broadcast across all checkpoint-engine workers, parameter by parameter in a pipeline so memory stays small, and each inference worker takes only the shard it needs. K2 reports a full parameter update in under 30 seconds. NeMo RL ships a comparable checkpoint-engine refit for non-colocated vLLM, moving weights with NIXL over UCX or RDMA.

That design deliberately sends more bytes than needed. A toy comparison: Qwen2.5-32B (65.5 GB in BF16) served by an engine that splits the model 8 ways across 8 nodes. Shard-to-shard resharding delivers each node its 8.2 GB; a full broadcast delivers all 65.5 GB to every node, 8x the minimum (at 400 GB/s per node, 0.16 s versus 0.02 s of transfer). K2's report says broadcasting everything transfers several times more data than the optimal approach but fully decouples the training and inference engines, and in practice beats transfer-what-you-need because there is less synchronization and better use of the bandwidth. It is the same trade as HybridFlow's in reverse: fewer bytes and more coupling, or more bytes and simpler code.

Low-precision rollout halves the sync but changes the policy. Serving FP8 weights (1 byte per parameter) sends half the BF16 bytes, but every sync now runs a quantization step (a scale factor per tensor or per block of weights maps values into FP8's narrow range), and the engine samples from a rounded copy of the trainer's weights. That gap is a deliberate source of training-inference mismatch, the subject of lesson 8.

blocks.code:
# trainer side (rank 0 of the weight-update group)
for name, tensor in gathered_hf_state_dict():      # full BF16 tensors
    dist.broadcast(tensor, src=0, group=update_group)

# engine side (SGLang), called by the controller
engine.init_weights_update_group(
    master_address=addr, master_port=port,
    rank_offset=1, world_size=1 + n_engine_ranks,
    group_name="weight_update_group", backend="nccl")
engine.update_weights_from_distributed(
    names=names, dtypes=dtypes, shapes=shapes,
    group_name="weight_update_group",
    flush_cache=True)   # drop KV/prefix cache built with old weights
blocks.caption: Sketch of a full-weight NCCL refit into SGLang. The engine method names and arguments are from SGLang's Engine class; the trainer loop is simplified.

blocks.md: After new weights land, cached KV entries are wrong: they were computed by the old weights. SGLang's `update_weights_from_distributed` flushes the cache by default, and AReaL's interruptible workers discard KV caches and recompute them with the new weights before continuing unfinished sequences.

Sync cost = bytes / bandwidth + resharding. The bytes are fixed by model size and precision; good systems avoid gathering the full model anywhere, send each rank only its shard, and keep the transfer off the critical path.

blocks.question: Training uses TP 8, and generation could reuse TP 8 (the setting HybridFlow attributes to NeMo-Aligner). Why might a system still choose to reshard to TP 2 for generation, despite the transition cost?
options: TP 2 uses less weight-sync bandwidth across the network
Larger TP is not supported by vLLM
Resharding makes the weights smaller
Generation is memory-bound; fewer shards per replica means more independent replicas, each decoding a large batch, and HybridFlow measured 60.3% lower generation latency for 7B at TP 2
blocks.explain: With TP 8 a 7B model's decode steps are tiny per GPU and spend time on communication. Smaller TP gives 4x more independent replicas with large batches. HybridFlow found TP 2 best for 7B; going lower failed to help because a smaller TP needs more KV cache per GPU.

blocks.question: A disaggregated run broadcasts a 70B BF16 model (140 GB) from one trainer rank over a single 400 Gb/s NIC every step. Roughly how long is the transfer at line rate, and what is the cheapest big improvement?
options: 0.35 s; nothing to improve
2.8 s; send disjoint shards from many trainer ranks in parallel so many NICs carry the load
28 s; switch to FP32 to avoid conversions
280 s; checkpoint to shared storage instead
blocks.explain: 140 GB at 50 GB/s is 2.8 s. The transfer is limited by one NIC. Sending shards from many trainer ranks in parallel (8 NICs gives 0.35 s), shard-to-shard resharding, or overlapping the sync with generation all help; FP32 doubles the bytes.

blocks.question: Kimi K2 broadcasts the full parameter set to every checkpoint-engine worker, although each inference worker needs only a shard. Why accept several times more bytes?
options: Inference engines cannot accept shards, only whole checkpoints
Broadcasting compresses the weights, so it moves fewer bytes in the end
It decouples the trainer's and engine's sharding from each other, and the simpler pipelined broadcast used the bandwidth better than transfer-what-you-need
It is required for FP8 rollout
blocks.explain: The report trades bytes for simplicity: each engine slices what it needs from a complete copy, so neither engine has to know the other's layout. It also says this beat the shard-exact approach in practice because of reduced synchronization overhead and higher bandwidth utilization, giving updates under 30 s for a 1T model.

lessons.title: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup

blocks.md:
Overlapping rollout and training breaks a simple assumption: that the data was sampled by the policy being trained. Three policies are in play, following AReaL's decoupled PPO and verl's rollout-correction docs:

- $\pi_{behav}$: the **behavior** policy, the weights the rollout engine actually sampled with (possibly several versions for one trajectory).
- $\pi_{prox}$: the **proximal** policy, a recent version that anchors the *trust region*: the band of ratios from $1-\epsilon$ to $1+\epsilon$ around it (the clip range $\epsilon$ is typically 0.2), inside which PPO's clip lets an update move each token's probability. Synchronous PPO and GRPO call this $\pi_{old}$.
- $\pi_\theta$: the policy being optimized now.

**Staleness** is how many optimizer steps separate the behavior policy from the current one.

Even "synchronous" training is slightly off-policy. DeepSeek-R1-Zero generated 8192 outputs per rollout and split them into 16 mini-batches of 512, training a single inner epoch (one pass over the 8192 outputs, one update per mini-batch): by the 16th mini-batch, the policy has taken 15 updates since the data was sampled. Another source is numerical: verl's docs list differences in precision (FP8, BF16) and backends (vLLM, SGLang, FSDP, Megatron) that make $\pi_{rollout}$ (verl's name for the behavior policy, as the rollout engine computes it) differ from the trainer's $\pi_{old}$ even with identical weights, and warn that ignoring this mismatch can lead to training collapse. Lesson 8 measures that gap and corrects it.

blocks.title: Three schedules and the policy version behind each batch

scenes.caption: Synchronous: batch 1 is sampled by v0, then trained into v1, then synced. Staleness is 0, but each pool idles while the other works (128 s rollout, 128 s train, 4 s sync, as in lesson 4).
One-step overlap: while the trainer turns b1 into v1, the rollout pool samples b2 with v0. b2 is then trained into v2 although it came from v0: staleness 1. Both pools stay busy.

Fully async, AReaL style, in steady state: generation never stops and the trainer consumes batches made earlier. When new weights arrive, in-flight sequences pause, reload, recompute their KV cache and continue, so one trajectory can mix versions.

blocks.md: Systems bound staleness explicitly. NeMo RL's async GRPO tags each trajectory with the weight version that generated it; with `max_trajectory_age_steps: 1`, a trajectory from v10 may be used at training step 10 or 11 and is discarded at step 12. AReaL limits how far generation may run ahead: with policy version $i$, $N_r$ trajectories generated so far, training batch $B$ and maximum staleness $\eta$, the rollout controller only submits new requests while

blocks.caption: In words: the batch the newest trajectory falls into, floor((N_r - 1) / B) counting from 0, may be at most eta versions ahead of i, so N_r is at most (i + eta + 1) B. At i = 10, B = 512, eta = 2: at most 6656, 1536 (3 batches) beyond the 5120 consumed. eta = 0 is synchronous.

blocks.md:
The objective must account for staleness. AReaL uses a decoupled PPO objective: the clip is centered on the recent proximal policy, and a separate importance weight corrects from the behavior policy to the proximal one. In AReaL the proximal policy is simply the parameters before each update, so the trainer recomputes $\pi_{prox}$ logprobs on each batch.

Why keep a separate proximal policy at all? Hilton, Cobbe and Schulman (2021) pointed out that PPO's $\pi_{old}$ does two jobs. It is the policy that sampled the data, which the importance correction needs, and it is the anchor that limits how far one update moves, which only needs to be *some recent* policy. Fusing the two makes PPO sensitive to how the data was batched and how old it is. In their words, "it matters how old the proximal policy is, but it does not matter whether or not the proximal policy was used for sampling". Decoupling them lets stale data be reweighted while the trust region stays around a fresh policy.

Why a ratio corrects anything: *importance sampling*. To average a quantity $f$ under a policy $p$ using samples drawn from a different policy $q$, weight each sample by $p/q$: the average under $q$ of $(p/q) \cdot f$ is $\sum q \cdot (p/q) \cdot f = \sum p \cdot f$, which is the average under $p$. Tokens that $p$ likes more than $q$ did count more, and the average comes out as if $p$ had sampled. Engines return log-probabilities, so each ratio is computed as $e$ to the power of a difference of logprobs, $\exp(\log p - \log q)$. In the objective below, $a_t$ is token $t$, $s_t$ the prompt and the tokens before it, $\hat A_t$ the token's advantage and $\epsilon$ the clip range.

blocks.tex: J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{a_t \sim \pi_{behav}}\Big[\sum_t \frac{\pi_{prox}}{\pi_{behav}} \min\big(u_t \hat A_t,\ \mathrm{clip}(u_t, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon)\hat A_t\big)\Big],\quad u_t = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}{\pi_{prox}(a_t\mid s_t)}
blocks.caption: AReaL equation 5. Each token's term is the importance weight pi_prox / pi_behav times PPO's clipped term, with u comparing the current and proximal policies. Naive PPO would instead clip the single ratio pi_theta / pi_behav, centering the trust region on the stale policy.

blocks.title: Four tokens from a stale trajectory, advantage +1, eps 0.2

scenes.caption: Each token has three logprobs: under the behavior policy that sampled it, the proximal policy (weights before this update) and the current policy.
w = exp(prox - behav) corrects for the policy having moved since sampling: 1.051, 0.905, 1.000, 1.492. AReaL does not clip it.
u = exp(theta - prox) is the trust-region ratio: 1.051, 1.350, 0.951, 1.105. Token 1 exceeds 1 + eps = 1.2, so with a positive advantage its term is clipped.
Decoupled terms w x min(u, clip(u)) for A = +1: 1.105, 1.086, 0.951, 1.649. Token 1 becomes 0.905 x 1.2; only token 1 loses its gradient.
Naive PPO clips exp(theta - behav) instead: 1.105, 1.200, 0.951, 1.200. Token 3 is now clipped too, although the current policy is only 10.5% above the proximal one on it.

blocks.prompt: Token 3 has logprobs -2.0 (behavior), -1.6 (proximal) and -1.5 (current). Naive PPO uses the ratio exp(-1.5 - (-2.0)) = 1.649. With advantage +1 and eps = 0.2, does naive PPO still push this token's probability up? Does the decoupled objective?
blocks.reveal: Naive PPO: the ratio 1.649 exceeds 1.2, so the clipped term wins and the token contributes a constant 1.2 with **no gradient**. The policy is held near a stale version it has already moved past. Decoupled: $w = e^{0.4} = 1.492$ reweights the sample, and $u = e^{0.1} = 1.105$ is inside $[0.8, 1.2]$, so the term is $1.492 \times 1.105 = 1.649$ and still has a gradient. The trust region is measured from where the policy is now, not from where it was when the data was sampled.

blocks.md:
What does it buy? Reported results, each on its authors' own setup:

- **AReaL**: up to 2.77x less end-to-end training time than synchronous systems on the same GPUs, with matched or better accuracy on math and code (models up to 32B, max staleness 4 for code and 8 for math).
- **Asynchronous RLHF** (Noukhovitch et al., ICLR 2025): an LLaMA 3.1 8B chatbot trained about 40% faster than a synchronous run with matching final performance; online DPO (direct preference optimization), which trains on pairs of responses marked better and worse instead of on scalar rewards, with online meaning the pairs are fresh samples from the current policy, was the most robust to off-policy data among the methods tested.
- **verl's fully async recipe** ([docs](https://github.com/verl-project/verl-recipe/tree/main/fully_async_policy), now in the verl-recipe repository) reports 2.35x to 2.67x for Qwen2.5-7B on 128 GPUs, combining staleness control, streaming and partial rollout.

Two newer designs show how far disaggregation goes. **StreamRL** (Zhong et al., 2025) is disaggregated from the start. *Stream generation* sends each sample to the trainer as soon as it finishes, so training starts once it has enough samples to fill its GPUs. For the long tail, a small fine-tuned *ranker* model predicts which prompts will produce long outputs (it recalls the top 20% longest with nearly 90% accuracy), and those go to dedicated instances with small batches, where each token decodes faster; regular samples share large batches. Separate pools also allow different GPUs: the paper notes an H20 has more memory bandwidth than an H800 for about 35% of the cost. Reported: up to 2.66x throughput, and up to 1.33x cost-effectiveness across datacenters.

**LlamaRL** (Meta, 2025) is a single-controller framework on native PyTorch that moves generation to its own GPUs, trains asynchronously with 1 to n steps of delay corrected by an importance-weighted objective (AIPO), and syncs weights GPU to GPU over NVLink in about 2 seconds for terabyte-scale models. Reported: up to 10.7x speedup over DeepSpeed-Chat-like systems for a 405B policy.

How big should each pool be? Use lesson 4's model: one step needs $W_r$ = 6144 GPU-seconds of rollout and $W_t$ = 2048 of training on 64 GPUs. With $x$ rollout GPUs and $64 - x$ trainer GPUs running overlapped, the step takes as long as the slower pool, $\max(W_r/x,\ W_t/(64-x))$, which is smallest when both are equal: $x = 64\,W_r/(W_r+W_t) = 48$, a 128 s step. In throughput terms, if a rollout GPU produces $g$ tokens per second and a trainer GPU consumes $h$, the rollout share of GPUs is $h/(g+h)$. Responses lengthen during reasoning RL, so $W_r$ grows and a fixed split drifts out of balance, which is why StreamRL rescales its generation pool.

blocks.title: Sizing the rollout pool on 64 GPUs (simplified model)

scenes.caption: With 6144 and 2048 GPU-seconds the curves cross at 48 rollout GPUs, AReaL's 75/25 split: both pools take 128 s and neither waits.
Responses get 1.5x longer (Wr = 9216). At 48 rollout GPUs the step is now 192 s while the trainer idles a third of it; the new balance point is about 52 GPUs and 176 s.
Simplified: both pools scale linearly and switching costs are ignored. Real decode throughput per GPU drops as each GPU's batch shrinks (lesson 4's last tip).

blocks.md: Staleness is a dial, not a free lunch. Too tight a bound and the system stalls behind long trajectories again (AReaL notes small eta slows generation and recommends a large one); too loose and updates use data from much older policies, which prior work shows can degrade learning. Importance weights can also explode for tokens the behavior policy found unlikely, which is why verl truncates or rejects extreme ratios (lesson 8).

Asynchrony converts idle GPU time into staleness. Every async system pairs a staleness bound (versions tracked per trajectory) with an objective that knows which policy sampled each token: an importance weight from behavior to proximal policy, and a trust region around a recent policy.

blocks.question: NeMo RL async GRPO runs with max_trajectory_age_steps: 1. A trajectory was generated with weights v10. At which training steps can it be used?
options: Steps 10 and 11; at step 12 it is discarded
Only step 10
Steps 9, 10 and 11
Any step, as long as importance sampling correction is on
blocks.explain: The docs' own example: a trajectory generated with v10 can be used for training steps v10 or v11, and at step v12 it is too old and is discarded. Importance correction handles the remaining mismatch; it does not remove the age limit.

blocks.question: In an async system, the rollout engine returns its own token logprobs. A developer uses them directly as pi_old in a standard PPO loss and skips recomputing anything on the trainer. Which problem does verl's rollout-correction doc warn about?
options: None: rollout logprobs are always identical to trainer logprobs
The KL penalty becomes negative
It silently assumes pi_rollout equals pi_old, but precision and backend differences (and staleness) make them differ, which can destabilize training
Rollout logprobs are in base 2 instead of base e
blocks.explain: verl calls this a common implementation mistake: treating the rollout policy as the PPO anchor without accounting for the gap between pi_rollout and pi_old. Its fixes are a decoupled mode with an importance weight from rollout to old policy, or a bypass mode that uses the rollout policy as the anchor explicitly.

blocks.question: Your synchronous colocated run spends 80% of each step in rollout, and one response in each batch runs to the 32k cap. Which plan addresses the root cause with the least algorithmic risk first?
options: Fully async with staleness 16 and no importance correction
Add training GPUs
Partial rollouts or a one-step overlap with bounded staleness and decoupled importance weights, then measure accuracy against a synchronous baseline
Lower the cap to 2k tokens
blocks.explain: The root cause is waiting on the long tail. Partial rollouts or a small, bounded staleness keep GPUs busy while keeping data nearly on-policy, and the decoupled objective corrects what remains. Large unbounded staleness risks learning quality; more trainers do not touch rollout; a tight cap truncates real reasoning.

blocks.question: A disaggregated async run uses 48 rollout and 16 trainer GPUs. Over training, average response length doubles while training cost per step only rises 10%. What happens, and what is the fix?
options: Nothing changes: asynchrony hides any imbalance
The rollout pool becomes the bottleneck and the trainer waits for data; move GPUs from training to rollout (or scale rollout out), as StreamRL does elastically
The trainer becomes the bottleneck; add trainer GPUs
Staleness drops to zero, so the importance weights can be turned off
blocks.explain: Overlap only hides the faster pool. Rollout work roughly doubles, so W_r/x grows past W_t/(64-x) and the trainer idles. The balanced split is x = 64 W_r/(W_r + W_t), which moves toward rollout as W_r grows; StreamRL monitors both stage times and scales generation out when it falls behind.

lessons.title: Training-inference mismatch: same weights, different logprobs

blocks.md: Weight sync just finished, so engine and trainer hold bit-identical weights. The engine samples a token and reports its logprob as -4.00. The trainer recomputes it for the loss and gets -3.00. Both are correct programs. The root is numerical (the deterministic-inference course goes deeper): floating-point addition is not associative, and kernels pick reduction orders from tensor shapes, so the same input in a different batch gives different bits (Thinking Machines sampled one prompt 1000 times at temperature 0 and got 80 distinct completions). RL adds a bigger gap: the sampler and the trainer are different programs.

Sources of mismatch, all with identical weights:

- **Different kernels and reduction orders**: vLLM or SGLang versus Megatron or FSDP, plus the serving engine's batch-dependent numerics.
- **Precision**: an FP8 rollout engine samples from a rounded copy of a BF16 trainer.
- **MoE routing**: a router picks its top-k experts by comparing scores, so a tiny numeric difference can switch which experts run. On Qwen3-30B-A3B the R3 paper measured about 10% of router decisions differing between training and inference, and 94% of tokens using a different expert in at least one layer.

Staleness from lesson 7 adds a further gap on top. To the trainer they all look the same: the behavior policy is not the policy it recomputes.

Why it bites: the trainer's PPO ratio assumes the data came from its own $\pi_{old}$, so a mismatch is an off-policy gap that nothing corrects, the "common implementation mistake" verl's docs name. Thinking Machines show it end to end on an RLVR run (Qwen 2.5-VL 8B, 4096-token rollouts): without an off-policy correction the reward collapses, with a loss spike around step 318 and a matching spike in sampler-trainer KL. With an importance-weight correction training proceeds smoothly, and with bitwise-identical sampler and trainer (batch-invariant kernels) the KL stays exactly 0.

Measure it before fixing it. Return the engine's per-token logprob with every sample, recompute it on the trainer, and log the gap. NeMo RL logs `token_mult_prob_error`, the mean of $e^{|\Delta|}$ over tokens, which should sit near 1: its guide says a steep upward trend past about 1 to 2% usually means a problem with how weights are updated, and spikes suggest an engine bug or a buggy refit. It also logs `gen_kl_error`, the KL from generation to policy, which it reports is empirically about 1e-3, treating values below 1e-3 as acceptable and spikes above it as worth investigating. verl's rollout correction has a metrics-only mode logging `rollout_corr/kl`, `rollout_corr/log_ppl_abs_diff` and `rollout_corr/chi2_token`.

blocks.tex: \rho_t = \frac{\pi_{train}(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{roll}(a_t \mid s_t)} = e^{\,\log\pi_{train} - \log\pi_{roll}},\qquad \text{mult error} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_t e^{|\log\pi_{train} - \log\pi_{roll}|},\qquad k_3 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_t \big(\rho_t - \log\rho_t - 1\big)
blocks.caption: rho is the per-token importance ratio from rollout to trainer. k3 is Schulman's KL estimator: every term is at least 0, and its average equals the KL from the rollout to the trainer distribution in expectation.

blocks.title: Five tokens: engine versus trainer logprobs

scenes.caption: Same weights, two programs. The gaps are exaggerated for the toy; real dense-model gaps give a mult error near 1.01.
ratio = exp(trainer - engine): 0.980, 1.051, 1.350, 2.718, 0.407. Token 3 is e times likelier under the trainer; token 4 is 0.41 times as likely.
Truncated importance sampling caps each weight at C = 2: only token 3 changes. Every token still contributes, with bounded variance and some bias.
Rejection (masking) with the band [0.5, 2] drops tokens 3 and 4 from the loss instead. Fewer samples, but no token outside the band can steer the update.

blocks.code:
import math
roll  = [-0.10, -2.30, -0.70, -4.00, -1.20]  # engine logprobs
train = [-0.12, -2.25, -0.40, -3.00, -2.10]  # trainer, same weights
rho = [math.exp(t - r) for r, t in zip(roll, train)]
print("ratio", [round(x, 3) for x in rho])
print("TIS  ", [round(min(x, 2.0), 3) for x in rho])          # cap C = 2
print("keep ", [0.5 <= x <= 2.0 for x in rho])                # reject band
print("mult error", round(sum(math.exp(abs(t - r))
      for r, t in zip(roll, train)) / 5, 3))
print("k3 KL", round(sum(x - math.log(x) - 1 for x in rho) / 5, 4))
print("k1 KL", round(sum(r - t for r, t in zip(roll, train)) / 5, 4))
blocks.caption: Runs as is. Output: ratio [0.98, 1.051, 1.35, 2.718, 0.407], TIS [0.98, 1.051, 1.35, 2.0, 0.407], keep [True, True, True, False, False], mult error 1.72, k3 KL 0.2152, k1 KL -0.086. A negative k1 on five tokens shows why the always-positive k3 is the better estimator on small samples.

blocks.md:
The fixes, roughly from cheapest to most thorough:

1. **Truncated importance sampling (TIS)**: weight each token by $\min(\rho_t, C)$. verl's docs use $C = 2$ as the example and give 1.5 to 5 as typical for token level. Token-level weights are low-variance but biased when the gap is large.
2. **Masked importance sampling or rejection**: drop tokens or whole sequences whose ratio leaves a band. A sequence ratio is the product of its token ratios, so verl also offers a *geometric-mean* filter, $(\prod_t \rho_t)^{1/T}$, with tight bounds such as 0.999 to 1.001.
3. **Sequence-level ratios** (GSPO, taught in the grpo-rlvr course), motivated by MoE instability.
4. **Remove the cause**: router replay for MoE (below), batch-invariant kernels for a bitwise match, or FP16 instead of BF16 on both sides, which [Qi et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26788) report largely eliminates the mismatch.

In verl these are presets of one rollout-correction module, in decoupled (three-policy) or bypass mode.

blocks.title: Why long sequences need a per-token (geometric) test

scenes.caption: With a 1% average gap per token, the sequence ratio passes 2 at 70 tokens and reaches about 20,959 at 1000. A sequence cap would reject every long chain of thought.
Even a 0.2% gap crosses 2 at about 347 tokens. The geometric mean stays at r for any length, so its bounds can be tight and fair to long answers.
A trainer that finds tokens 1% less likely shrinks the product toward 0 just as fast, so a lower bound such as 0.5 has the same length trap.

blocks.md: **Router replay (R3)** removes the MoE part at the source. The engine records, for every token and MoE layer, which experts it routed to, and returns them with the sample. In the trainer's logprob and training forward passes, each router uses that recorded top-k as its mask but still computes the softmax gate weights from its own router logits, so gradients keep flowing into the router. Routing masks for a shared prefix are identical, so they can be cached alongside the prefix KV cache, which keeps multi-turn rollouts cheap. The paper reports only a 3.45% end-to-end throughput cost. NeMo RL asks vLLM for the experts with `enable_return_routed_experts=True` and requires prefix caching to stay on. Do not confuse R3 with the *Routing Replay* the GSPO paper used (grpo-rlvr course): that one reuses the trainer's routing from the logprob pass in the update, to cancel routing changes caused by updates. R3 replays the engine's routing in both trainer passes, so it also removes the engine-versus-trainer gap.

blocks.tex: g^{replay}_i = \frac{I^{infer}_i \, e^{s^{train}_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{M} I^{infer}_j \, e^{s^{train}_j}}, \qquad y^{replay} = \sum_{i=1}^{M} g^{replay}_i \, E_i(x^{train})
blocks.caption: R3, equations 9 and 10. I^infer is the 0/1 mask of the K experts the engine chose, s^train the trainer's router logits, E_i the i-th of M experts. The mask comes from inference; the weights and gradients come from training.

blocks.title: Training-inference KL with and without router replay

scenes.caption: R3 paper: estimated token KL of 15.35e-4 for Qwen3-30B-A3B versus 6.4e-4 for dense Qwen3-8B. Replay brings the MoE model to 7.5e-4, near the dense one.
NeMo RL's Nemotron-3.5 recipe, a different model and metric (gen_kl_error): 8.6e-4 without replay, 3.7e-4 with it. Compare bars within each source only.

blocks.md: Averages hide the damage, which comes from rare tokens. NeMo RL's guide shows one token that vLLM gave a logprob near -5 and the trainer near -15: a 10-nat gap, a ratio of $e^{-10} = 4.5 \times 10^{-5}$. With the $k_3$ estimator that single token contributes about 9 to the generation-side KL and about 22,015 to the policy-side KL, dominating every average. Without router replay, in NeMo RL's Nemotron recipe, 0 to 2 tokens per step disagreed by 10 to 31 nats and spiked the mean `token_mult_prob_error` to 1e6 to 3e9 on about 20% of steps; with replay it stayed near 1.010.

"Same checkpoint" does not mean on-policy. Two engines with identical weights are two different policies at the level of logprobs, and the gap grows with FP8 rollout, MoE routing and long sequences. Treat the rollout engine as a behavior policy and log the gap every step.

Log engine and trainer logprobs per token; watch mult error and KL; correct with truncation or masking (geometric for long sequences); remove the causes you can, with router replay for MoE and batch-invariant kernels when a bitwise match is worth the speed.

blocks.question: A run with FP8 rollout and a BF16 trainer collapses after about 300 steps; the same run with BF16 rollout does not. What should you do first?
options: Raise the learning rate so the policy moves past the noise
Switch the trainer to FP8 so both sides match exactly
Increase the clip range epsilon
Log per-token engine and trainer logprobs (mult error, KL), then add a rollout correction such as token-level TIS or masking
blocks.explain: FP8 rollout makes the behavior policy a rounded copy of the trainer's, an uncorrected off-policy gap that can grow until training collapses, as in the Thinking Machines run. Measure the gap first; then truncate or mask extreme ratios. A trainer in FP8 does not make the two programs bitwise equal, and a wider clip range lets more of the mismatch through.

blocks.question: An MoE policy shows a few tokens per step with 10+ nat gaps between engine and trainer, while dense models trained on the same stack do not. Which fix targets the cause?
options: Router replay: record the engine's routed experts and use them as the trainer's top-k mask
A larger TIS cap
Longer responses
More reference-model KL
blocks.explain: Different expert choices mean the two sides ran different sub-networks for that token, which produces gaps far beyond rounding noise. Replay makes the trainer use the experts the engine actually used, while gate weights still come from training logits. Truncation only limits the damage of each bad token.

blocks.question: A rejection filter drops sequences whose ratio product leaves [0.5, 2]. Per-token gaps are tiny, but the run stops learning from long answers. Why, and what helps?
options: Long answers are wrong more often
The product of many near-1 ratios drifts past the bounds as length grows; use the geometric-mean ratio with tight bounds
The filter only looks at the first token
Rejection needs FP32 logprobs
blocks.explain: A sequence ratio is a product over tokens, so a 1% average gap compounds to about 2.7x at 100 tokens. Long sequences get rejected for being long, not for being off-policy. The geometric mean normalizes by length, so the same per-token gap scores the same at any length.

lessons.title: Multi-turn agentic rollouts: tools, servers and token-in, token-out

blocks.md: So far a rollout was one long generation. An agentic rollout interleaves generation with tools: the model writes 600 tokens and a code call, a sandbox runs it for 8 seconds, the output is appended, the model writes again. While the sandbox runs, that trajectory has nothing for the GPU. The agentic-rl-environments course covers what the environment does and how the loss treats tool text; this lesson covers the infrastructure that keeps GPUs busy and the token ids exact.

A toy model, generated by a seeded script: 16 trajectories, 3 turns each. Each turn decodes 150 to 1500 tokens at 20 ms per step (3 to 30 s), and after turns 1 and 2 a tool call takes 1 to 20 s. As in lesson 3, decode step time is assumed not to depend on how many sequences run. Two schedulers:

- **Batch per turn**: decode turn 1 for all 16, wait for the slowest, run all tool calls, wait for the slowest, and so on.
- **Independent coroutines**: each trajectory runs its own loop against an inference server with continuous batching, which takes any sequence that is ready.

blocks.prompt: Under batch per turn the turns take 30, 27 and 29 s of decoding and the tool phases 19 and 20 s. The longest single trajectory needs 87 s end to end. How long does each scheduler take, and how busy is the GPU?
blocks.reveal: Batch per turn: 30 + 19 + 27 + 20 + 29 = **125 s**, and the GPU decodes for 86 s of it, **68.8%**; during each tool phase no sequence is decoding. Independent coroutines: every trajectory proceeds as soon as its own tool returns, so the batch ends when the longest trajectory does, **87 s**, 30% sooner, and some sequence is always decoding.

blocks.title: Three of the 16 trajectories under both schedulers (toy model)

scenes.caption: Batch per turn: each turn starts only when every trajectory's previous step is done. Gaps are waiting; during tool phases the GPU has nothing to decode (125 s, 68.8% busy).
Independent coroutines: each trajectory alternates on its own clock. Trajectory 11 finishes at 33 s; the batch ends at 87 s and the GPU always has someone to decode.

blocks.code:
import asyncio, random, time
random.seed(7)
N, TURNS, SCALE = 16, 3, 0.01   # 1 simulated second = 10 ms
dec = [[round(random.randint(150, 1500) * 0.02) for _ in range(TURNS)] for _ in range(N)]
tool = [[random.randint(1, 20) for _ in range(TURNS - 1)] for _ in range(N)]

async def generate(i, k):        # server call; continuous batching assumed
    await asyncio.sleep(dec[i][k] * SCALE)

async def run_tool(i, k):        # sandbox or web call, no GPU
    await asyncio.sleep(tool[i][k] * SCALE)

async def batch_per_turn():
    for k in range(TURNS):
        await asyncio.gather(*(generate(i, k) for i in range(N)))
        if k < TURNS - 1:
            await asyncio.gather(*(run_tool(i, k) for i in range(N)))

async def agent_loop(i):         # one coroutine per trajectory
    for k in range(TURNS):
        await generate(i, k)
        if k < TURNS - 1:
            await run_tool(i, k)

async def independent():
    await asyncio.gather(*(agent_loop(i) for i in range(N)))

for name, fn in [("batch per turn", batch_per_turn), ("independent", independent)]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); asyncio.run(fn())
    print(f"{name}: {(time.perf_counter() - t0) / SCALE:.0f} simulated s")

blocks.md: Real systems split this into **clients and servers**. Agent loops are clients: cheap CPU coroutines that call tools and keep the conversation. Inference engines are servers. In verl, an `AgentLoop` per prompt calls `LLMServerClient.generate`, which sends the first turn to the server with the fewest requests and every later turn of the same request id to the *same* server (a sticky session). Stickiness matters because that server already holds the conversation's prefix in its KV cache, so with prefix caching only the new tool output and the next turn need prefill (the paged-attention-prefix-caching course explains the cache). [Agent Lightning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03680) goes further: the trainer exposes an OpenAI-like endpoint per task, and the agent runs anywhere, without GPUs.

blocks.title: Server-based rollout for agents

scenes.caption: Turn 1 of conversation 7 goes to the least-loaded server. Server 1 now holds its prefix in KV cache.
Turn 2 of conversation 7 returns to server 1 (sticky), so only the tool output and new tokens need prefill. Other conversations keep server 2 busy.
Tools run in their own pools. Kimi K2 deploys heavy environments as dedicated services that scale independently and runs many concurrent rollouts to hide slow interactions.
Finished trajectories go to the trainer as exact token ids with a loss mask. Long ones can be paused and resumed in the next iteration (K2 uses partial rollouts here too).

blocks.md: **Token-in, token-out.** Most agent frameworks call an LLM through a chat API: messages in, text out. That is fine for serving and wrong for training. verl's agent-loop docs report that the token ids from re-applying the chat template to the final messages may not equal the ids actually sampled, for two reasons. A tool parser rewrites content: it lifts the text inside `<tool_call>` tags into a structured field, and encoding the edited message does not reproduce the original tokens. And decode then encode is not reversible: in the Agent-R1 report verl links, the model sampled `<`, `think`, `>` as three tokens and re-encoding the text produced `<th`, `ink`, `>`. The trainer would then compute logprobs for tokens the policy never sampled. verl observed that applying the chat template to the final history kept PPO from converging even in single-turn training, so its servers take prompt token ids and return response token ids.

blocks.title: One trajectory as the trainer must see it (toy tokens and ids)

scenes.caption: Prompt, a tool call, the tool's output, then the answer: one sequence. The ids are invented for the toy.
Each token has an author. Prompt and tool output were written by the environment; the rest was sampled by the policy.
The loss mask is 1 on sampled tokens and 0 on prompt and tool tokens (verl's response_mask). The model still reads tool tokens as context.
The model sampled "1" then "2" (ids 16, 17). Re-encoding the text could produce a single token "12" instead: every later position shifts and the trainer scores a token the policy never chose.

blocks.md: Tool tokens get mask 0 because the policy did not choose them: training on them would push the model to predict tool output instead of improving its own actions (the agentic-rl-environments course, lesson 2, goes deeper). Here the point is plumbing: the client keeps prompt ids, response ids and a response mask in step with what the server returned, turn by turn, along with the engine's logprobs for each sampled token. Those logprobs are the behavior policy for lesson 8's corrections, and they matter more in multi-turn runs, where a trajectory can span many minutes, partial rollouts and weight versions.

Agentic rollouts move the bottleneck from decode length to tool latency. Run each trajectory as its own coroutine against continuous-batching servers, route a conversation's turns to the same server, scale tools as separate services, and pass exact token ids and logprobs to the trainer.

A common misconception is that storing the chat transcript is enough, because the trainer can tokenize it again. Tokenizing is not the inverse of sampling: the policy may have sampled a non-canonical split, and tool parsers edit messages. Train on the ids the engine returned.

blocks.question: A multi-turn trainer stores each conversation as chat messages and re-applies the chat template to build training tokens. Why can this silently make training off-policy?
options: The chat template adds a system prompt, which doubles the loss
The re-encoded ids can differ from the sampled ids (parser edits, non-canonical splits, special tokens), so the loss scores tokens the policy never produced
Chat templates cannot represent tool calls
Re-tokenizing is too slow for training
blocks.explain: The gradient should raise or lower the probability of choices the policy actually made. If the ids differ, logprobs and masks refer to a different sequence, and the importance ratios compare two policies on tokens neither sampled. verl saw PPO fail to converge this way, hence token-in, token-out APIs.

blocks.question: In the toy model, tool waits grow from 1 to 20 s to 10 to 60 s. Which change keeps the inference GPUs busiest?
options: Batch per turn with a larger batch
A tighter maximum response length
Move tools onto the GPU servers
Run many more concurrent trajectories as independent coroutines, so some are always decoding while others wait on tools
blocks.explain: With independent loops, GPU idleness comes only from too few trajectories being ready to decode. More concurrent trajectories fill the gaps, which is what Kimi K2 does with a large number of concurrent rollouts; batch per turn keeps a global idle phase for every tool round.
